# Education in Sweden
Sweden's education system is structured around a nine-year comprehensive compulsory school (grundskola) covering ages 6–16, followed by an elective three-year upper secondary school (gymnasieskola). The compulsory school is divided into lower (grades 1–3), middle (4–6), and upper stages (7–9), where students study 16 compulsory subjects including Swedish, mathematics, English, and sciences. Grades start from year 6 using an A–F scale, with national tests in grades 3, 6, and 9 to ensure assessment standards. After compulsory school, almost 99% of students enroll in upper secondary school, choosing among 18 national programmes split into preparatory and vocational tracks, with varying specializations from natural sciences to arts and trades.
Higher education in Sweden complies with the Bologna Process, offering degrees at bachelor's, master's, and doctoral levels through universities and university colleges. Admission requires proficiency in Swedish and English and may include the Swedish Scholastic Aptitude Test (SweSAT). There is a growing independent school (friskolor) sector publicly funded but privately operated, including for-profit and religious schools, drawing about 10% of pupils. Sweden provides extensive student aid and emphasizes anti-discrimination policies in education. The system has faced challenges like declining PISA scores linked partly to immigration, testing irregularities, and debates over independent school impacts on equality. Preschool education is free for children from age three with a focus on play and foundational skills, supporting parental employment.
